Dossier 1: Nepal. Facts: no criminalisation of gender identity/expression; same-sex legal since 2007; third gender markers; LGR procedure messy but resident-facing (not visitor). Documented social hostility: discrimination in public spaces, government institutions, physical and sexual harassment in provincial cities; anti-LGBTQ sentiment gaining momentum; leader's homophobic video; death threats. But no trans-specific criminal law; no documented police targeting of trans people specifically; societal acceptance mixed — some acceptance, education curriculum, pride parades. Violence: harassment documented, no killing rate. Traveler-facing: no border friction documented, no facility bans. Resident-facing gaps (LGR procedure, healthcare) don't count.

So D1: weakest feature is tier 3-ish: documented societal hostility with thin recourse? Actually there is recourse in the sense of functioning courts (Supreme Court rulings in favor), but harassment in provincial cities. Documented social acceptance exists (third-gender tradition, pride, education). Score maybe ~0.55-0.60. Hmm. Let's think: no criminalisation of trans identity, no police targeting documented, no facilities restrictions, no border friction. Social hostility documented at ground level (harassment in public spaces and government institutions, physical/sexual harassment in provincial cities), plus rising anti-LGBTQ political hostility. That's tier 3 with partial recourse. Not tier 1. I'd place around 0.55-0.62. Given documented acceptance-tradition plus hostile ground-level reports... Nepal. I'd say 0.58.

Dossier 2: high court read down sodomy laws in 2024, no GI protection, no union recognition, police dismissive of anti-LGBT violence (2011 source, and 2019 claim police refused to investigate attack because gay people considered criminals). Documented violence: a 2010 killing, hate crimes. No trans-specific data at all — thin on trans. So: decriminalised same-sex conduct recently; no trans-specific law, no trans-specific violence documented; police dismissive toward LGBT victims (dated 2011 & 2019). Also 2011 signatory to joint statement; bishop against criminalisation. No laws criminalising gender expression. But there's a recent decriminalisation (2024) — climate improving. Thin trans data: extrapolate. Same-sex conduct now legal (read down), so no criminal lever for the state against gender-nonconforming people in principle; but police dismissiveness documented, dated. No facility/border rules. I'd put this around 0.55-0.60. Compare with D3 (PNG-like): sodomy 14 years, police violence against trans people documented as primary perpetrator — clearly lower, maybe 0.25-0.30.

D2 vs D1: D1 has no criminalisation and documented embedded third-gender tradition; D2 has a recently read-down sodomy statute, no trans data, dismissive policing. Hmm. D2's homosexuality decriminalisation is a secondary factor anyway. D1 emerges with more documented acceptance (third gender tradition documented, pride, curriculum) but more documented hostility (anti-LGBTQ political momentum, harassment). D2 has thin trans data → extrapolate from: recent decriminalisation, civil society, dismissive police (dated), violence against perceived gay/gender-nonconforming people (a killing in 2010). Hmm.

I'd give D1 ~0.58, D2 ~0.55. Roughly similar. Let me differentiate: D2's most recent trans-relevant signal is a 2024 decriminalisation and no documented trans-specific harm; but police non-investigation of anti-LGBT violence is a tier-3 with thin recourse — though dated (2011, 2019). D1 has present-day (2024) reported physical and sexual harassment of trans people in public spaces and government institutions, and 2026 political hate speech with death threats. D1 also has institutional positives (Supreme Court rulings, third gender official documents, pride faces). I think D1 slightly above D2? Actually the death threats and rising hostility in D1 (2026) is recent and serious. Hmm, but no state action.

Both roughly Elevated Risk band. Let me set D1 = 0.56, D2 = 0.58? Let me think about what best reflects. Actually D2's dossier: no trans-specific anything; decriminalised same-sex; police dismissive of violence against LGBT (dated). The absence of trans data in a thin-data jurisdiction → extrapolate toward risk implied by structure: recent judicial decriminalisation, no GI discrimination law, no union recognition, dismissive policing, documented violence against gender-nonconforming people. That resolves to maybe 0.50-0.55.

D1: Nepal has documented police...? Not really police targeting. Documented official third-gender recognition, courts working for trans people. But also documented ongoing harassment and anti-trans political hostility. D1 has more documented positives operating (courts, official documents, education, community orgs). I'd put D1 slightly higher, maybe 0.60. Hmm, but the ground-level report of discrimination in government institutions and frequent physical/sexual harassment in provincial cities is real. And note the subnational paragraph. I'd say D1 = 0.58, D2 = 0.54.

Dossier 3: PNG-analogue. Sodomy up to 14 years, sporadically enforced (arrests 2022; prosecutions against LGBTQ). Police are a main source of violence against MSM and trans people; gay men sexually abused/raped/beaten by police; abuse continues when reported; victims framed as perpetrators. Nearly no accountability for violence generally (sorcery killings, police impunity). No LGR. Presence of third-gender traditions (palopa) — some cultural acceptance, a sanctuary village. Traveler-facing: police violence against trans people = tier 2 (state-tolerated/state-directed targeting by police). Plus reinforced by general impunity. Score maybe 0.25-0.30. Since criminalisation sporadically enforced, and police violence documented against trans people specifically. I'd say 0.27.

Dossier 4: Portugal-like. Legal, marriage equality, self-ID (resident-facing — climate signal), GI discrimination prohibited, conversion practices banned, facilities access protected (traveler-facing positive!), hate-crime law with GI grounds in force and operating. Roll-back bills in first reading (2026) — unresolved, so not yet law. Recent relevant: 2006 murder of trans woman, invoked; but old. Public support high. Facilities access protected is a documented traveler-facing positive. So the rating: high, Reduced/Low band. Roll-back risk is pending, unresolved → light weight but a climate signal. Score maybe 0.78-0.82. Given protected facilities access, hate crime aggravation enforced, no criminalisation, no border friction documented. But active legislative attack (first reading) with a governing party pushing it — that's a present political climate signal of hostility at the state level, though not law yet. And the ombudsman requesting constitutional review of the hate-speech provision (institutional watchdog questioning). Hmm. I'd place 0.78. Maybe 0.80. The pending roll-back is unresolved; rule 4 says don't let open questions out-vote known goods. I'll go 0.79.

Dossier 5: Cameroon-like? Facts: private same-sex legal; public same-sex expression punished 6 months-2 years; local org documented arrests prompted by false accusations of same-sex intercourse, and mistreatment and torture of LGBTQ people by law enforcement. No LGR; no anti-discrimination; societal discrimination entrenched, concealment; no known LGBTQ orgs (though one registered). Trans-specific: no trans-specific rules documented; assessed against documents as issued; gender identity not addressed in data-protection law. Law enforcement mistreatment and torture of LGBTQ documented by local civil-society org (undated). Arrests prompted by false accusations. General context: extrajudicial killings, torture by security forces; impunity; custody conditions unknown.

Traveler-facing exposure: an outed trans visitor with documents mismatching; police mistreatment of LGBTQ people documented (tier 2), arrests documented. Plus societal hostility with concealment. Score: low, maybe 0.25-0.30. Compare D3: D3 has sodomy statute enforced sporadically + documented police rape/beatings of trans people specifically + near-total impunity. D5: public same-sex affection criminalised (6 months-2 years) which can apply to a trans person traveling with a partner publicly; documented arrests on false accusations; torture by law enforcement; entrenched discrimination; but D5 also has more rule-of-law state? Actually the 2012 report documents extrajudicial killings, torture, rape by security forces — that's a severe impunity context.

Which is worse? D3 has explicit trans-specific police violence (trans people raped/beaten by police in the capital) — extremely on-point. D5 has LGBTQ mistreatment/torture by police but no trans-specific documentation, and criminalisation only of public affection. Hmm. D3 also has sodomy statute 14 years. I'd rank D3 slightly worse: 0.25 vs D5 0.30. Or roughly equal. Let me think about the public-affection statute in D5: a trans visitor displaying affection could be jailed; plus police torture of LGBTQ; no LGR meaning documents assessed as issued. And the presence of false-accusation arrests as a police lever against LGBTQ people — that's exactly a lever used. I'd say D5 = 0.27, D3 = 0.24. Hmm, close.

Actually consider D3's subnational: a sanctuary village where trans people live openly; and third-gender traditions. That's some documented acceptance. D5 has no documented trans acceptance at all, issues taboo, "imported from another region". But D5 lacks a specific trans violence record; D3 has police sexual violence against trans people.

Rule 20: local vulnerability is not traveller risk—but police rape/beatings of trans people in the capital is street-level and involves police, applies to any visibly trans person including a visitor. That's tier 2. D5's police torture of LGBTQ is also tier 2 by analogy.

I'll give D3 0.25 and D5 0.27. Or maybe D3 0.26, D5 0.28. Fine.

Now D1 vs D2 ordering. Let me reconsider D2 more carefully. Decriminalisation 2024 (read down), no GI protection law, no unions, police dismissive of anti-LGBT violence (2011 academic submission; 2019 claimant's account). Violence: 2010 killing of a man perceived gay; hate crimes suspected. Trans-specific: nothing. So the worst documented feature is tier 3 (societal hostility with thin recourse) — but even that is mostly dated and not trans-specific. Non-trans-specific criminalisation resolved. Extrapolating: recently decriminalised, some civil society, diplomatic commitments, religious authority against criminalisation. Perhaps 0.55-0.60.

D1's worst documented feature: ongoing (2024) harassment and physical/sexual violence against visibly trans people in provincial cities and government-institution discrimination, plus 2026 political hate speech/death threats. That's tier 3 hostility, ongoing. But counterweight: strong institutional positives with actual trans-specific operation (Supreme Court ordering recognition, third-gender official documents, education curriculum, pride). Under rule 13, "a jurisdiction whose dossier shows (i) no trans-specific criminal offence, (ii) no documented targeting of trans people by police... and (iii) documented social acceptance of gender diversity (an embedded third-gender tradition) sits above jurisdictions with similar formal machinery but no documented acceptance." So D1 sits above D2. D1 ≈ 0.60, D2 ≈ 0.53.

Hmm, is 0.60 too high given documented harassment? Rule 19: social hostility has real weight. But harassment in provincial cities is described as frequent. Traveler in Kathmandu would face less. Subnational weighting: capital-versus-periphery. I'll set D1 = 0.58, D2 = 0.53.

Then D4 = 0.79, D3 = 0.25, D5 = 0.28.

Let me sanity-check D4 vs the band: Reduced/Low boundary 0.80. D4 has functioning protections for facilities access and hate crime, high acceptance, but an active roll-back in first reading with parliamentary majority by governing party + allies (that's a real state-level threat signal) and an ombudsman questioning the hate speech provision. Also a 2006 murder (dated). I'd say 0.78. That's within Reduced Risk band, near the top.

Final: 1: 0.58, 2: 0.53, 3: 0.25, 4: 0.78, 5: 0.28.
